newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank says German inflation under control.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank says German inflation under control.

text.p: German inflation is under control even though money supply growth is faster than the target rate, the Bundesbank said on Tuesday, adding that its key task now was to keep prices down.
The German central bank said in its December report that M3 money supply growth might exceed its target growth rate of four to seven percent at the end of this year.

October data showed M3 expansion of 8.4 percent from the fourth quarter of 1995, still well outside the range, and the Bundesbank said the pace of monetary expansion had accelerated somewhat in recent months.
"It is possible that the money supply goal will also be exceeded at the end of the year," the Bundesbank said.
But it said it expected the rate of expansion to slow as temporary factors, such as high public lending, faded.
"As these influences recede, money supply growth should weaken again," it said, adding the stronger-than-expected growth did thus not present an inflationary danger.
Even relatively strong growth in the German economy currently did not signal danger for price stability, it said.
"Germany has conclusively reached the goal of price stability. For the Bundesbank it is now a question of securing this success long-term," the central bank said.
Exchange rate levels broadly reflected economic fundamentals and the mark had apparently completely corrected from a prolonged period of strength.
"Unlike 1995, exchange rate levels now to a large degree correspond to economic fundamentals," the central bank said.

Turning to European Economic and Monetary Union, the Bundesbank said Germany's state and regional governments must save more so the country could meet the entry criteria to join Europe's planned currency union in 1999.
"In order to avoid running the risk of exceeding the Maastricht Treaty criteria next year, it is imperative to work on making sure that budgets are not exceeded," it said.

Nations must present 1997 economic data showing their budget deficts do not signifcantly exceed the Maastricht Treaty reference value of three percent of total gross domestic product if they want to be among the first to join the union.
"The reduction of deficits is absolutely imperative in order to improve the framework for economic activity," the Bundesbank said.
More importantly, it will be necessary to ensure that the consolidation efforts will be durable and that more progress can be achieved in the longer term, it added.
